newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Economists slam unreliable S.African trade data.
newsitem.headline: Economists slam unreliable S.African trade data.

text.p: Financial markets on Thursday cheered the major turnaround in South Africa's trade account in July which helped to push yields on the bond market sharply lower.
But the data drew scant applause from economists who said the indicator was unreliable and meaningless.

According to South African Revenue Service (SARS) data released on Thursday, South Africa recorded a trade surplus of 2.58 billion ($573 million) rand in July, up from a 27.6 million rand deficit in June and more than three times economists' most optimistic forecasts of an 800 million rand surplus.
No explanation was given by SARS for the sudden turnaround and officials at SARS' customs and excise division were unavailable for comment.
Edward Osborn, strategic economist at Edey Rogers & Co, said the data in no way reflected trade in a particular month because of the SARS system of accumulating figures.

"The method of accumulating the figures picks up any amendments to past figures, so if there are significant amendments to earlier months either by way of coverage or correction or valuation then all those corrections will be reflected in the current month," Osborn said.
"You can from time to time get a pretty shocking outcome of this process and I think this is one of those instances."

Constantin Vayenas, emerging markets economist at UBS in London, said the data was consistent with his view that South Africa's balance of payments would improve in the second half of 1996. "But it's a lot quicker than one would have expected."

Econometrix economist Tony Twine said that as the deficit on South Africa's current account of its balance of payments was one of the main reasons that the rand was struggling to find a level at the moment, reliable trade account data was critical.

"The service deficit is a fairly constant number, so the trade figures become critical in taking a view on the rand and if they are of extremely dubious validity it just makes life doubly difficult," he said.
Twine noted that the data's release after a hefty 6.9 billion rand current account in the first half suggested the J-curve was "kicking with a vengeance not previously imagined".
The J-curve predicts the positive reaction of a country's trade balance following a currency devaluation such as the rand has undergone this year.
"By some miracle that might be happening, but I very much doubt it," Twine said.
Osborn said there needed to be a radical revision of the way the monthly data was determined.
"The whole process is absolutely wrong and I think it calls for a radical revision. I think this is an outrage quite frankly," Osborn said.

However, the data helped yields on South Africa's capital market move to their best levels since the beginning of August, with the key R150 issue falling to an intraday low yield of 15.26 percent from 15.41 percent on Wednesday.
